questions.question:
Answer Questions Q1.07.4 and Q1.07.5 using the following data. Cayley-Hamilton Theorem states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Consider a matrix: \[A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Express the given matrix \(A\) as a product of two triangular matrices, \(L\) and \(U\), where the diagonal elements of the lower triangular matrix \(L\) are unity and \(U\) is an upper triangular matrix. \[a = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 5 \\ 4 & 8 & 13 \\ 6 & 27 & 31 \end{bmatrix}\]
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Given the \(3 \times 3\) square matrix \(A\) (notated as \(a\) in the problem text): \[A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 5 \\ 4 & 8 & 13 \\ 6 & 27 & 31 \end{bmatrix}\] We decompose \(A\) into a product of a unit lower triangular matrix \(L\) and an upper triangular matrix \(U\) using Doolittle's algorithm (\(A = LU\)): \[\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 5 \\ 4 & 8 & 13 \\ 6 & 27 & 31 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ l_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ l_{31} & l_{32} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12} & u_{13} \\ 0 & u_{22} & u_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & u_{33} \end{bmatrix}\] Step 1: Determine the first row of \(U\) (multiply first row of \(L\) by columns of \(U\)): \[u_{11} = 2, \qquad u_{12} = 1, \qquad u_{13} = 5\] Step 2: Determine the first column of \(L\) (multiply remaining rows of \(L\) by first column of \(U\)):
  • \(l_{21} u_{11} = 4 \implies l_{21}(2) = 4 \implies l_{21} = 2\)
  • \(l_{31} u_{11} = 6 \implies l_{31}(2) = 6 \implies l_{31} = 3\)
Step 3: Determine the second row of \(U\):
  • \(l_{21} u_{12} + u_{22} = 8 \implies (2)(1) + u_{22} = 8 \implies u_{22} = 6\)
  • \(l_{21} u_{13} + u_{23} = 13 \implies (2)(5) + u_{23} = 13 \implies u_{23} = 3\)
Step 4: Determine the remaining entries of \(L\) and \(U\):
  • For \(l_{32}\): \[l_{31} u_{12} + l_{32} u_{22} = 27 \implies (3)(1) + l_{32}(6) = 27 \implies 6l_{32} = 24 \implies l_{32} = 4\]
  • For \(u_{33}\): \[l_{31} u_{13} + l_{32} u_{23} + u_{33} = 31 \implies (3)(5) + (4)(3) + u_{33} = 31\] \[15 + 12 + u_{33} = 31 \implies 27 + u_{33} = 31 \implies u_{33} = 4\]
Assembling the final factored matrix architectures: \[L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad U = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\] \[\boxed{LU = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}}\]

questions.explanation: Given, \[v(t)= \begin{cases} 2~\text{V}, & 0\le t\le 2~\text{s} \\ 0, & t>2~\text{s} \end{cases}\] The current increases linearly from \(0\) to \(2~\text{A}\) during the first \(2~\text{s}\). A resistor cannot satisfy the given waveforms because for a resistor, \[v=Ri\] and the voltage and current must have the same waveform. A capacitor cannot satisfy the given waveforms because \[i=C\frac{dv}{dt}\] and a constant voltage would imply zero current. Now Inductor, \[v=L\frac{di}{dt}\] The slope of the current waveform is \[\frac{di}{dt} = \frac{2-0}{2-0} = 1~\text{A/s} = \text{constant}\] i.e. from 0 to 2 second v(t) is constant. Substituting the given values, \[2=L(1) \ \Rightarrow \ L=2~\text{H}\] After \(t=2~\text{s}\), \[v=0\] and the current remains constant at \(2~\text{A}\), which is consistent with the behavior of an ideal inductor since \[v=L\frac{di}{dt}=0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{di}{dt}=0\] Hence, \[\boxed{\text{Inductor, }2~\text{H}}\]

questions.question: A \(10\text{V}\) battery with an internal resistance of \(1\ \Omega\) is connected across a nonlinear load whose V-I characteristic is given by \(7I = V^2 + 2V\). The current delivered by the battery is A.
questions.explanation: The terminal voltage across the nonlinear load is \[V=E-Ir\] \[V=10-I \tag{1}\] The load characteristic is \[7I=V^2+2V \tag{2}\] Substituting (1) into (2), \[7I=(10-I)^2+2(10-I)\] \[7I = 120-22I+I^2\] \[I^2-29I+120=0\] \[(I-24)(I-5)=0\] Therefore, \[I=24~\text{A} \qquad \text{or} \qquad I=5~\text{A}\] For \[I=24~\text{A} \quad \Rightarrow \quad V=10-24=-14~\text{V}\] which is not admissible for the given nonlinear load as load is delivering power to battery in this case. and for, \[I=5~\text{A} \quad \Rightarrow \quad V=10-5=5~\text{V}\] Hence, the valid operating point is \[\boxed{I=5~\text{A}}\] Therefore, \[\boxed{5}\]

questions.question: An ideal voltage source will charge an ideal capacitor
questions.explanation: For a capacitor, \[i=C\frac{dv}{dt}\] When an ideal capacitor is connected directly across an ideal voltage source, the capacitor voltage must immediately become equal to the source voltage. The charging time constant is \(\tau = RC\) Since both the voltage source and capacitor are ideal, \(R=0\) Therefore, \[\tau = RC = 0\] A zero time constant implies that the capacitor reaches its final voltage instantaneously. Equivalently, \[v_C(0^+)=V \qquad \text{which requires}, \frac{dv}{dt}\rightarrow\infty\] and hence \[i=C\frac{dv}{dt}\rightarrow\infty\] An ideal voltage source can supply this impulse current. Therefore, the capacitor charges instantaneously. Hence, \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }\text{Instantaneously}}\]

questions.explanation:
To find \(V_{\text{th}}\):
Open-circuit terminals \(A\) and \(B\). Since the terminals are open-circuited, the current through the \(4\Omega\) resistor is zero. Applying KVL, \[-10+V_s+V_{\text{th}}=0 \ \Rightarrow \ V_{\text{th}}=10-V_s \tag{1}\] By KCL, \[\frac{V_{\text{th}}-10}{2} = 4V_s \ \Rightarrow \ V_{\text{th}} = 8V_s+10 \tag{2}\] From (1) and (2), \[10-V_s=8V_s+10 \ \Rightarrow \ V_s=0\] Hence, \[\boxed{V_{\text{th}}=10~\text{V}}\] To find \(R_{\text{th}}\):
Deactivate the independent \(10\text{ V}\) source and apply a \(1\text{ V}\) test source across terminals \(A\) and \(B\). Let the current supplied by the test source be \(I\). Applying KCL, \[\frac{-V_s}{2} -4V_s +\frac{-V_s-1}{4} =0\] \[-2V_s-16V_s-V_s-1=0 \ \Rightarrow \ 19V_s=-1\] \[V_s=-\frac{1}{19}\text{ V}\] The test-source current is \[I = \frac{1-(-V_s)}{4} = \frac{1-\dfrac1{19}}{4} = \frac{9}{38}\text{ A}\] Therefore, \[R_{\text{th}} = \frac{1}{I} = \frac{38}{9} = 4.22~\Omega\] \[\boxed{ V_{\text{th}}=10~\text{V}, \qquad R_{\text{th}}=4.22~\Omega }\]

questions.explanation:
To find Norton resistance \(R_N\):
Deactivate the independent sources The two \(3\Omega\) resistors connected between the middle node and terminal \(B\) are in parallel. \[R_N = 3+\left(3\parallel 3\right)= 3+\frac{3\times3}{3+3}\] \[R_N = 3+1.5 = 4.5\Omega\] To find Norton current \(I_N\):
Short-circuit terminals \(A\) and \(B\). Transform the \(2\text{ A}\) source in parallel with \(3\Omega\) into an equivalent voltage source: \[V=IR=2\times3=6\text{ V}\] Applying KVL in Loop 1, \[-6+3I_1+3(I_1-I_N)=0 \ \Rightarrow \ 6I_1-3I_N=6 \tag{1}\] Applying KVL in Loop 2, \[3(I_N-I_1)+3I_N-6=0\] \[6I_N-3I_1=6 \tag{2}\] Solving (1) and (2), \[I_1=I_N=2\text{ A}\] Therefore, \[\boxed{ I_N=2\text{ A}, \qquad R_N=4.5\Omega }\]

questions.question: A major advantage of active filters is that they can be realized without using
questions.explanation: A major advantage of active filters is that they can be realized without using inductors. In conventional passive RC/RLC filters, inductors are bulky, expensive, non-ideal at low frequencies, and difficult to fabricate on Integrated Circuits (ICs). Positive Half Cycle (\(V_{\text{in}} > 0\)):
During the positive half cycle of the input signal \(4\sin 10t\):
  • The voltage at the inverting terminal is greater than at the non-inverting terminal (\(V_- > V_+\)).
  • The op-amp output goes to negative saturation (\(-V_{\text{sat}}\)).
  • The buffer transmits this negative voltage to the FET gate, turning the FET OFF.
  • No current flows through resistance \(R\), resulting in: \[V = 0\,\text{V}\]
Negative Half Cycle (\(V_{\text{in}} < 0\)):
During the negative half cycle of the input signal:
  • The voltage at the inverting terminal is less than at the non-inverting terminal (\(V_- < V_+\)).
  • The op-amp output goes to positive saturation (\(+V_{\text{sat}}\)).
  • This turns the FET ON, creating a low-resistance path between drain and source.
  • The voltage across resistance \(R\) connected between \(+12\,\text{V}\) and \(-12\,\text{V}\) becomes: \[V = 12\,\text{V} - (-12\,\text{V}) = 24\,\text{V}\]
\[\boxed{V = 0\,\text{V} \text{ (Positive Half Cycle)}, \quad V = 24\,\text{V} \text{ (Negative Half Cycle)}}\]

Oscillator Identification:
The given circuit is a Wien-Bridge Oscillator. The frequency of oscillation for a Wien-Bridge oscillator is given by the formula: \[f = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}\] Given values: \[R = 1\,\text{k}\Omega = 10^3\,\Omega, \quad C = 4.7\,\mu\text{F} = 4.7 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{F}\] Substituting the values into the formula: \[f = \frac{1}{2\pi \times (4.7 \times 10^{-6}) \times 10^3} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 4.7 \times 10^{-3}}\] \[f \approx 33.863\,\text{Hz}\] \[\boxed{33.863}\]

questions.question: A first order system is initially at rest and excited by a step input at time \(t = 0\). Its output becomes \(1.1\,\text{V}\) is in \(4\) seconds and eventually reaches a steady state value of \(2\,\text{V}\). Determine its time constant
questions.explanation: The step response of a first-order system initially at rest is given by the standard formula: \[c(t) = C_{\text{ss}}\left(1 - e^{-\frac{t}{\tau}}\right)\] \[1.1 = 2\left(1 - e^{-\frac{4}{\tau}}\right)\] \[e^{-\dfrac{4}{\tau}} = 0.45\] \[\tau = \frac{4}{\ln(0.45)} \approx \boxed{5\,\text{s}}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The system represented by the transfer function \[G(s) = \frac{s^2 + 10s + 24}{s^4 + 6s^3 - 39s^2 + 19s + 84}\] has how many pole (s) in the right-half \(s\)-plane.
questions.explanation:
The Characteristic Equation (\(\text{C.E.}\)) is: \(s^4 + 6s^3 - 39s^2 + 19s + 84 = 0\) Constructing the Routh-Hurwitz array: \[\begin{array}{c|ccc} s^4 & 1 & -39 & 84 \\ s^3 & 6 & 19 & 0 \\ s^2 & \frac{(6)(-39) - 19}{6} = -42 & 84 & \\ s^1 & \frac{(-42)(19) - (84)(6)}{-42} = +11 & 0 & \\ s^0 & 84 & & \end{array}\] The number of sign changes in the first column is \(2\). Therefore, there are \(2\) poles present in the right-half of the \(s\)-plane. \[\boxed{2}\]
Key points
Default Assumption: Whenever it is written just "transfer function" and the nature of feedback is not mentioned, by default assume it to be a closed-loop transfer function.

The equivalent capacitance is \[C=\frac{C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2}+C_3.\] Here, \[C_1=\frac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}{\dfrac{d}{2}}, \qquad C_2=\frac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_2\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}{\dfrac{d}{2}}, \qquad C_3=\frac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_3\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}{d}.\] Substituting, \[C= \frac{ \left(\dfrac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1A}{d}\right) \left(\dfrac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_2A}{d}\right) }{ \dfrac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1A}{d} + \dfrac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_2A}{d} } + \frac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_3A}{2d}.\] Hence, \[C= \frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d} \left( \frac{\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2}{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2} +\frac{\varepsilon_3}{2} \right).\] Substituting \[\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\,\text{F/m}, \quad A=400\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2, \quad d=20\times10^{-2}\,\text{m},\] \[\varepsilon_1=1, \qquad \varepsilon_2=2, \qquad \varepsilon_3=4,\] gives \[C= \frac{8.85\times10^{-12}\times400\times10^{-4}} {20\times10^{-2}} \left[ \frac{1\times2}{1+2} +\frac{4}{2} \right].\] \[C=4.72\times10^{-12}\,\text{F} =4.72\,\text{pF}.\] \[\boxed{4.72}\]

questions.question: Determine the electric field intensity at the point \(p\) for the arrangement shown in figure above [figure unavailable]
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] Since \(R\gg a\), the distance of point \(P\) from all the charges can be approximated as \(R\). The electric field due to charge \(Q_1\) is \[\vec{E}_1 = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q_1}{R^2}\,\hat{a}_y = 9\times10^9 \times \frac{2000\times10^{-12}}{1^2} \,\hat{a}_y = 18\,\hat{a}_y\;\text{V/m}.\] Since the distances of \(Q_2\) and \(Q_3\) from \(P\) are equal and \[|Q_2|=|Q_3|,\] their magnitudes of electric field are equal. \[|\vec{E}_2| = |\vec{E}_3| = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q_2}{R^2} = 9\times10^9 \times \frac{1000\times10^{-12}}{1^2} = 9\;\text{V/m}.\] Since \(Q_3\) is negative, the electric field at \(P\) is directed towards \(Q_3\), whereas for the positive charge \(Q_2\), it is directed away from the charge. Hence, the vertical components of \(\vec{E}_2\) and \(\vec{E}_3\) cancel each other, while their horizontal components add. From the geometry, \[\cos\theta = \frac{B}{H} = \frac{a/2}{R} = \frac{1}{200}.\] Therefore, \[\vec{E} = \vec{E}_1+\vec{E}_2+\vec{E}_3 = E_1\hat{a}_y + 2E_2\cos\theta\,\hat{a}_x.\] Substituting, \[\vec{E} = 18\,\hat{a}_y + 2\times9\times\frac{1}{200}\,\hat{a}_x = \left(0.09\,\hat{a}_x+18\,\hat{a}_y\right)\,\text{V/m}.\] Hence, \[\boxed{\vec{E}=\left(0.09\,\hat{a}_x+18\,\hat{a}_y\right)\,\text{V/m}}\]
Key points
  • For \(R\gg a\), all source-to-observation distances may be approximated as \(R\).
  • Electric field due to a point charge is \[\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{R^2}\,\hat{a}_R.\]
  • Use symmetry to identify cancelling and reinforcing components.
  • Resolve inclined electric fields into horizontal and vertical components before vector addition.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not forget that the field due to a negative charge is directed towards the charge.
  • Do not add electric field magnitudes directly; perform vector addition.
  • Use the approximation \(R\gg a\) only after identifying the direction of each field.
  • Ensure that \[\cos\theta=\frac{a/2}{R}\] is used for the horizontal component.

questions.question: A square coil of turns and \(10\,\text{cm}\) side is moved through a steady magnetic field of \(1\,\text{Wb/m}^2\) at a constant velocity of \(2\,\text{m/sec}\) with its plane perpendicular to the field as shown in figure. Plot the variation of induced e.m.f as the coil moves along the field. [figure unavailable]
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] The loop of side \(a=10\,\text{cm}\) moves with velocity \[v=2\,\text{m/s}\] through a magnetic field of flux density \[B=1\,\text{Wb/m}^2\] When the loop has entered the magnetic field by a distance \(x\), \[\text{Overlapping area}=ax\] \[\phi=B(ax)\] Hence, the induced emf is \[e=-\frac{d\phi}{dt} =-Ba\frac{dx}{dt}\] \[e=-Bav\] \[e=-1\times0.1\times2 =-0.2\,\text{V}\] When \[x=a\] the loop is completely inside the magnetic field region and the overlapping area becomes constant. \[\phi=BA=\text{constant}\] Therefore, \[e=0\] [figure unavailable] When the loop starts leaving the magnetic field region, \[\text{Overlapping area}=a(a-x)\] \[\phi=Ba(a-x)\] The induced emf becomes \[e=-\frac{d\phi}{dt} =Ba\frac{dx}{dt}\] \[e=Bav\] \[e=1\times0.1\times2 =0.2\,\text{V}\] Therefore, the induced emf waveform is \[e= \begin{cases} -0.2\,\text{V}, & 0<x<10\,\text{cm} \\ 0, & 10\,\text{cm}<x<20\,\text{cm} \\ +0.2\,\text{V}, & 20\,\text{cm}<x<30\,\text{cm} \end{cases}\] [figure unavailable]
Key points
  • Induced emf is given by Faraday's law: \(e=-\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\).
  • Flux is \(\phi=BA\) when the magnetic field is uniform.
  • While entering and leaving the field region, flux changes linearly with time, producing constant emf.
  • When the loop is completely inside the field region, flux remains constant and emf becomes zero.
Mistakes to avoid

Both the wire and the loop are coplanar. Determine the magnitude and direction of current in the loop that produces a zero flux density at its center.
questions.explanation: [figure unavailable] Total magnetic flux density at point \(O\) is zero. Magnetic flux density due to the long straight conductor is \[\vec{B}_{1} = \frac{\mu_{0} I_{1}}{2\pi R}\,\hat{a}_{x}\] Magnetic flux density due to the circular ring is \[\vec{B}_{2} = \frac{\mu_{0} I_{2}}{2r}\, \left(-\hat{a}_{x}\right)\] Since the net magnetic field at \(O\) is zero, \[\vec{B}_{1}+\vec{B}_{2}=0\] \[\frac{\mu_{0} I_{1}}{2\pi R}\,\hat{a}_{x} + \frac{\mu_{0} I_{2}}{2r} \left(-\hat{a}_{x}\right) = 0\] Therefore, \[\frac{I_{1}}{\pi R} = \frac{I_{2}}{r}\] \[I_{2} = \frac{I_{1} r}{\pi R}\] Given, \[I_{1}=1000\,\text{A}\] \[r=50\,\text{mm}\] \[R=1000\,\text{mm}\] Substituting, \[I_{2} = \frac{1000\times 50}{\pi \times 1000}\] \[I_{2} = 15.92\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{15.92}\]

Statement for Linked Questions (Q1.07.1 and Q1.07.2):
An inductor designed with \(400\) turns coil wound on an iron core of \(16\,\text{cm}^2\) cross sectional area and with a cut of an air gap length of \(1\,\text{mm}\). The coil is connected to a \(230\,\text{V}\), \(50\,\text{Hz}\) ac supply. Neglect coil resistance, core loss, iron reluctance and leakage inductance. \((\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\,\text{H/m})\)

The given figure shows a magnetic circuit formed by an ideal core material. Determine the magnetic flux density in the air gap. [figure unavailable]
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable]
Method 1
To determine the magnetic flux density(B) in the air gap, we use ampere's law for magnetic circuits. Given the magnetic circuit with two identical coils aiding each other, we first calculate the total Magnetomotive Force (MMF). \[\text{Total MMF} = 2 \times (N \times I) = 2 \times (10 \times 10) = 200\,\text{AT}\] For an ideal core, the reluctance of the core material is zero (\(\mathcal{R}_{core} = 0\)). Therefore, the entire MMF is dropped across the air gap. \[\text{MMF} = H \times g\] \[H = \frac{\text{MMF}}{g} = \frac{200}{4 \times 10^{-3}} = 50,000\,\text{A/m}\] The magnetic flux density (\(B\)) in the air gap is: \[B = \mu_0 \times H = (4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 50,000\] \[B = 0.02\pi \approx 0.0628\,\text{T} = 62.83\,\text{mT}\]
Method 2
Alternatively, we can solve using the concept of magnetic reluctance (\(\mathcal{R}\)). The MMF of each winding is \(10 \times 10 = 100\,\text{AT}\). Since the core is ideal, the only reluctance is offered by the air gap: \[\mathcal{R}_{ag} = \frac{l_{ag}}{\mu_0 A} = \frac{4 \times 10^{-3}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (10^{-2} \times 10^{-2})} \approx 0.3183 \times 10^8\,\text{AT/Wb}\] Total flux (\(\phi\)) passing through the air gap (sum of fluxes from both coils): \[\phi_{total} = \phi_1 + \phi_2 = 2\phi = 2 \times \frac{100}{0.3183 \times 10^8} = 6.283\,\mu\text{Wb}\] Flux density (\(B\)) in the air gap: \[B = \frac{\phi_{total}}{A} = \frac{6.283 \times 10^{-6}}{10^{-2} \times 10^{-2}} = 0.06283\,\text{Wb/m}^2\]
\[\boxed{0.0628}\]
Key points
  • Ideal Core: Means permeability \(\mu_r \to \infty\), thus reluctance \(\mathcal{R}_{core} = 0\).
  • Aiding Coils: When currents are in directions that produce flux in the same direction, MMFs are additive.
  • Flux Density: \(B = \mu_0 H\) in air or \(B = \phi / A\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure the cross-sectional area \(A\) is converted correctly to \(\text{m}^2\).
  • Do not forget to account for both coils if they are aiding each other.
  • The dimensions of the core and the "non-magnetic sleeve are not required for this specific calculation because core is ideal and the flux density is primarily determined by the air gap reluctance.

By decreasing the field flux, its speed is raised by \(20\%\) this also causes a \(10\%\) increase in load torque. Calculate the percentage change in field current. The armature resistance including the brushes is \(1\) Ohm. Neglect saturation and armature reaction.
questions.explanation:
Given, \[I_{a1}=40\,\text{A}\] Initial induced EMF is \[E_1=200-40\times1=160\,\text{V}\] Let the reduced flux be \[\frac{\phi_2}{\phi_1}=x\] Torque increases by \(10\%\), hence \[T_2=1.1T_1\] Since, \[T\propto \phi I_a\] \[\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{\phi_2I_{a2}}{\phi_1I_{a1}} = \frac{xI_{a2}}{40}\] \[\frac{xI_{a2}}{40}=1.1\] \[I_{a2}=\frac{40\times1.1}{x}\] New induced EMF is \[E_2=200-I_{a2}R_a = 200-\frac{44}{x}\] Speed increases by \(20\%\), therefore \[\omega_2=1.2\omega_1\] Also, \[E\propto \phi\omega\] \[E_2=x(1.2)E_1\] \[200-\frac{44}{x}=1.2x(160)\] \[192x^2-200x+44=0\] Solving, \[x=0.315,\;0.72\] For \(x=0.315\), current becomes very large. Hence permissible value is \[x=0.72\] Percentage reduction in flux is \[\frac{\phi_1-\phi_2}{\phi_1}\times100 = (1-0.72)\times100 = 28\%\] \[\boxed{28}\]
Key points
  • Reduction in flux increases speed but also changes armature current for the required torque.

The domestic load current before motor starting is \[I_L = 0.125\angle -36.86^\circ\ \text{p.u.}\] The 11-kV bus voltage during motor starting has already been obtained as \[V = 0.74\angle0.383^\circ\ \text{p.u.}\] The voltage at the domestic load terminals is obtained after accounting for the voltage drop across the feeder reactance of \(j0.05\) p.u., i.e., \[V_L = V-I_L(j0.05).\] The feeder voltage drop is \[I_L(j0.05) = 0.125\angle-36.86^\circ \times 0.05\angle90^\circ = 0.00625\angle53.14^\circ.\] Since phasor subtraction is most conveniently carried out in rectangular form, \[V = 0.74(\cos0.383^\circ+j\sin0.383^\circ) = 0.73998+j0.00495,\] and \[I_L(j0.05) = 0.00625(\cos53.14^\circ+j\sin53.14^\circ) = 0.00375+j0.00500.\] Therefore, \[\begin{aligned} V_L &= (0.73998+j0.00495) - (0.00375+j0.00500) \\ &= 0.73623-j0.00005. \end{aligned}\] Converting back to polar form, \[V_L = 0.7362\angle-0.004^\circ\ \text{p.u.}\] Thus, the domestic load voltage is \[\boxed{ V_L = 0.7362\angle-0.004^\circ\ \text{p.u.} }\] The percentage voltage reduction is \[\frac{1-0.7362}{1}\times100 = 26.38\%.\] Hence, \[\boxed{26.38\%}\]

questions.explanation: Reactance relays respond primarily to reactance and are relatively unaffected by fault resistance. Hence they are particularly suitable for earth-fault protection. \[\boxed{\text{(A)}\;\text{Earth faults}}\]

questions.question: The use of high-speed circuit-breakers
questions.explanation: High-speed circuit breakers clear faults rapidly. A lower fault-clearing time improves transient stability by increasing the critical clearing angle and critical clearing time. Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(B)}\;\text{Improves system stability}}\]

An SCR is connected in series with a \(300\,\text{V}\) ac supply and a \(300\) ohms load resistor. Calculate for a firing angle of \(45^\circ\), (a) the reading of a moving coil ammeter connected in series with the load, and (b) the reading on a moving iron voltmeter connected across the SCR.
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] Waveforms: [figure unavailable] (a) Reading of a moving coil ammeter
A moving coil ammeter measures the average value of the current. For a half-wave rectifier circuit with an SCR and a resistive load, \[V_{\text{avg}} = \frac{V_m}{2\pi}\left(1+\cos\alpha\right)\] At \[\alpha=45^\circ,\] \[V_{\text{avg}} = \frac{300\sqrt{2}}{2\pi} \left(1+\cos45^\circ\right) = 115.32\,\text{V}\] Hence, \[I_{\text{avg}} = \frac{V_{\text{avg}}}{R} = \frac{115.32}{300} = 0.384\,\text{A}\] (b) Reading of a moving iron voltmeter across the SCR
A moving iron voltmeter measures the RMS value of the voltage across the device. The voltage across the SCR is equal to the supply voltage when the SCR is OFF and is approximately zero when the SCR is ON. Therefore, \[V_{T,\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{2\pi} \left[ \int_{0}^{\alpha} \left(V_m\sin\omega t\right)^2\,d(\omega t) + \int_{\pi}^{2\pi} \left(V_m\sin\omega t\right)^2\,d(\omega t) \right] }\] Using \[\int\sin^2x\,dx = \frac{x}{2}-\frac{\sin2x}{4},\] we obtain \[V_{T,\mathrm{rms}} = V_m \sqrt{ \frac{1}{4\pi} \left[ \alpha - \frac{\sin2\alpha}{2} + \pi \right] }\] Substituting \[V_m=300\sqrt{2}\,\text{V}, \qquad \alpha=\frac{\pi}{4},\] \[V_{T,\mathrm{rms}} = 424.26 \sqrt{ \frac{1.25\pi-0.5}{4\pi} }\] \[V_{T,\mathrm{rms}} = 221.46\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{ I_{\text{avg}}=0.384\,\text{A}, \qquad V_{T,\mathrm{rms}}=221.46\,\text{V} }\]
Key points
  • A moving coil ammeter measures the average (DC) value of current.
  • A moving iron voltmeter measures the RMS value of voltage.
  • For a half-wave controlled rectifier, \[V_{\text{avg}} = \frac{V_m}{2\pi}(1+\cos\alpha).\]
  • The SCR voltage is equal to the source voltage during the blocking interval and nearly zero during conduction.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use RMS value when calculating the moving coil ammeter reading.
  • Do not forget that the SCR voltage is zero during its conduction interval.
  • Evaluate the RMS integral over the correct OFF intervals only.

If a diode is connected in anti-parallel with a thyristor, then
options: both turn-off power loss and turn-off time decrease
turn-off power loss decreases but turn-off time increases
turn-off power loss increases, but turn-off time decreases
questions.explanation:
When the diode turns ON, it reverse biases the thyristor. Hence, the stored charge in the thyristor is removed more quickly, making the turn-off process faster. However, since the diode conducts during the turn-off interval, additional current flows through the diode, which increases the turn-off power loss. \[\boxed{C}\]
Key points
  • An anti-parallel diode provides a reverse-bias path for the SCR during turn-off.
  • Reverse bias accelerates carrier removal, thereby reducing the SCR turn-off time.
  • Conduction through the diode during commutation increases the turn-off energy (power) loss.

Does not allow smooth reversal of load current, but reduces the response time
Allows smooth reversal of load current with improved speed of response
Flows only if there is no interconnecting inductor
questions.explanation: In a circulating current dual converter, both converters remain active simultaneously. An interconnecting reactor limits the circulating current between the converters. questions.question: A transfer instrument employed in the standardization of a polar type \(a.c\) potentiometer is _____
questions.explanation: [figure unavailable] A polar type AC potentiometer is standardized using a transfer instrument. A transfer instrument should: (i) work accurately on both AC and DC. (ii) give the same indication for equal RMS values of AC and DC. Thermal instruments satisfy these conditions because they operate on \[\text{Heating effect}\propto I^2R,\] which is independent of waveform. \[\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\text{ \begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Property} & \textbf{Electrostatic} & \textbf{Thermal} & \textbf{Dynamometer} & \textbf{PMMC} \\ \hline \text{Works on AC} & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & \times \\ \hline \text{Works on DC} & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark \\ \hline \text{Measures true RMS} & \times & \checkmark & \text{Approx.} & \times \\ \hline \text{Depends on waveform} & \text{Yes} & \text{No} & \text{Yes} & - \\ \hline \text{Frequency effect} & \text{Present} & \text{Negligible} & \text{Present} & - \\ \hline \text{Phase error} & \text{No} & \text{No} & \text{Yes} & - \\ \hline \text{Suitable for AC--DC transfer} & \times & \checkmark\ \text{Best} & \text{Possible} & \times \\ \hline \text{Principle} & \text{Electrostatic force} & I^{2}R\ \text{heating} & \text{EM torque} & \text{Magnetic interaction} \\ \hline \text{Main use} & \text{High voltage} & \text{RMS} & \text{Power measurement} & \text{DC measurement} \\ \hline \text{Preferred for AC potentiometer standardization} & \times & \checkmark & \times & \times \\ \hline \end{array} }}\] Therefore, \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }\text{a thermal instrument}}\]
